source.title: Uncovering Audio-Text Alignment in Large Audio-Language Models through Cross-Modal Concept Neurons
source.authors: Tzu-Quan Lin; Chih-Kai Yang; Yi-Cheng Lin; Hao Tang; Hung-Yi Lee

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies cross-modal attribute neurons in audio-language models, but it does not test whether neuron poles generally have one or two human-namable jobs, how explanation accuracy changes on held-out activations, or any of the other specified claim versions. Its cross-modal alignment and intervention findings are related to neuron-level analysis but do not measure those claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports neuron-overlap, steering, and deactivation results. They concern whether attribute-specific audio and text neuron sets overlap and affect audio recognition—not the share of neurons with one main job, the listed classic examples, attribution-graph reconstruction, or explanation scores on new activations. The related results are recorded with versions ["none"]. It also reports ambient cosine-similarity results, but those do not measure any listed version and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study identifies label-specific FFN neurons shared between audio and text inputs in three audio-language models and tests them by steering and zero-ablation. It does not audit what share of neurons have one main job, revisit classic polysemantic examples, build attribution graphs, or score neuron explanations on held-out activations. Its neuron sets are selected top-k by distinctiveness, so they say nothing about neurons in general. The paper neither tests nor relies on the claim. Its findings fit no listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that audio and text attributes align in label-specific FFN neurons, an alignment that cosine similarity over whole vectors barely reveals. Text-derived steering of these neurons changes audio recognition, and deactivating them selectively impairs it. How strongly models rely on this alignment varies, with DeSTA2.5-Audio weakest.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses neuron distinctiveness, cross-modal top-k overlap, activation steering, and zero-ablation in audio-language models; it is not a neuron-pole interpretability audit or an automated explanation test.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model and task: DeSTA2.5-Audio has weaker steering and no selective necessity window for animal and spoken-language tasks; Audio Flamingo 3's gender necessity window is selective in only 39% of bootstrap resamples. Audio-token-only interventions weaken effects but retain reported selectivity in the tested Qwen2.5-Omni emotion setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Top-k label-specific audio and text FFN neuron sets overlap far above random. They overlap more for matched than mismatched labels in all 9 testable model-task pairs (R1–R12).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In audio-language models, label-specific FFN neurons selected from audio and text inputs coincide, label by label, more than for mismatched labels.

fits_no_version.finding: Text-derived steering of cross-modal neurons beats matched random sets for 42/72 labels. The effect is weak in DeSTA2.5-Audio, at 7/24 labels (R13–R24).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Text-derived directions on cross-modal concept neurons change audio-attribute recognition, with strength depending on the model.

fits_no_version.finding: Zeroing cross-modal neurons impairs the target task before control tasks in 10/12 combinations. The exceptions are DeSTA2.5-Audio animal and language (R25–R36).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Audio-attribute recognition selectively depends on cross-modal concept neurons in most tested model-task combinations.

record.problems: The authors note limitations: only three LALMs and four fixed SAKURA attribute tasks were studied; DeSTA2.5-Audio differs from the other models in multiple ways, making the cause of weaker effects difficult to isolate; the gender task is binary; and steering neuron-set size was selected using deactivation windows located on the test split. Audio Flamingo 3's gender necessity window is also unstable under bootstrap resampling.
record.rows_left_out: No results bearing directly on the listed claim versions were left out. Ambient cosine-similarity results were omitted because they measure a related alignment comparison, not a listed claim version or the neuron-level findings cataloged here.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or of shares with one, two or unknown jobs.
Three 7–8B audio-language models, but no job-share estimate and no dense/MoE or scale comparison.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron analysis.
No comparison of architectures, regularization or tools against an interpretable-neuron share.
Steering and ablation of selected neuron sets only; no attribution graphs and no comparison with replacement models.
Does not test whether explanations from activating examples predict firing elsewhere.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses classification is correct. All rows rightly carry versions ["none"], and no row fixes are needed. Row states are relative to the study's own hypothesis, not to any claim version. Ambient cosine results (Table 1) were reasonably omitted. The neurons studied are selected top-k sets, not a population audit, so nothing here bears on the neuron-share claims.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles or estimate the share with one, two, or not-yet-understood jobs.
Uses three audio-language models but does not estimate the claimed job-count shares, or test their scaling across dense/MoE models or up to trillions of parameters.
Does not analyze InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons or test recursive generalization against superposition.
Does not compare architectures, regularization, or tools as causes of an interpretable-neuron share; it gives no InceptionV1-sized model estimates.
Does causal steering and neuron deactivation, but does not build attribution graphs or test whether they explain behavior without a replacement model or reconstruction error.
Does not test whether explanations fitted to activating examples predict firing on separate examples.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.
